To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the culture of organotypically developed, transfected cerebelar neurons in vitro is feasible and that such cells may be tracked in vivo at high resolution.

(i) cerebellar slices, maintained in culture for periods of up 14 days, can be used as an experimental tool to study the development, in vitro, of Purkinje cells, and (ii) the same Purkinje cells can be repeatedly observed, at high resolution, over extended periods of time, in the same culture.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the use of laser-scanning confocal microscopy for the repeated, high resolution, in vitro visualization of nuclear and cytosolic fluorescent signals, as a function in vitro development in cerebellar neurons.

the use of organotypic slice cultures of the cerebellum for the purposes of studying the molecular mechanisms underlying the development, differentiation, and function of Purkinje and other cerebellar neurons.
the development and application of a new culture system for the study of Purkinje cell development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present culture system, which is based on the use of collagen-coated membranes, permits the repeated, same-cell tracking of nuclear and/or cytoplasmic signals, in live, transfeced cerebellar neurons, as a function development in vitro, by use of laser confocal microscopy.

the system described here, using the 25 mm diameter Anodisc membrane, permits the repeated, same-cell visualization of dynamic cellular events within live Purkinje neurons, in cerebellar organotypic slice culture.
this culture system is an ideal tool for the repeated tracking of cellular events in live neurons, over extended periods of time, at high resolution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of organotypic cerebellar slices for the purposes for tracking dynamic cellular events, such as the nuclear localization of proteins, in the same live cells, as a function or development in vitro, has been defined.
we have developed a system that allows the repeated, high resolution, visualization of nuclear signals in the same live cell, in a developing, organotypic slice culture.

we have developed a system for the in vitro culture of cerebellar organotypic slices from postnatal mice, in which the same live cell may be observed by laser confocal imaging, repeatedly, over extended periods of time, and at high resolution, using water-immersion objectives.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the culture of organotypically developing slices of cerebellum, in the presence of the glia, is a useful system for the repeated, high resolution tracking of nuclear and cellular signals in live cells, over extended time frames, and that such tracking is not limited to the study of the developing cerebellum, but may be applied to any organotypic culture.
the culture of organotypics slices for the purposes for tracking dynamic cellular events, within the same live cells at high resolution, is feasible.

the culture of organotypice cerebellar slices is a useful model system in which to study the dynamics of gene expression and protein trafficking in live Purkinje neurons, over extended periods of development in vitro, and at high resolution.
